title: Fidan Rushes to Libya as Rivals Circle, Ankara Seeks Cluster Munition Transfer to Ukraine, Hormuz Impasse Drives Oil Past $100
subhead: Turkey's foreign minister lands in Tripoli and Benghazi to protect military and energy stakes as Washington pushes Libyan unification; a $256M arms package to Ukraine awaits US approval; and Brent crude tops $100 as Iran vows to keep Hormuz shut until Washington changes policy.

sections.heading: Fidan Flies to Libya as US-Backed Unification Push Accelerates
sections.body:
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan arrived in Libya on August 12 for a two-day visit spanning both Tripoli and Benghazi, according to Anadolu Agency. He met Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah and Libya's national security adviser in Tripoli, with talks covering Turkey-Libya ties, the political process, energy, and defense cooperation, Anadolu reported. Fidan was also scheduled to travel to Benghazi — the eastern power center controlled by Khalifa Haftar's forces — as Ankara seeks to preserve its military, maritime, energy, and commercial interests on both sides of Libya's divide.

The visit comes one day after a suspected assassination of a senior Libyan intelligence officer and amid a drone strike on the Zawiya refinery in western Libya that firefighters battled to contain, Reuters and AP reported. Al-Monitor noted that Fidan's dual-city itinerary is calibrated to counter a US-backed push to unify Libya's rival governments, which could reshape the power arrangements that anchor Turkey's presence in the country. The Libya Observer reported that Dbeibah and Fidan discussed supporting efforts to unify national institutions.

Ankara's stake is direct: the 2019 Turkey-Libya maritime boundary agreement, military deployments, and defense contracts all rest on relationships with the Tripoli-based government. Expanding outreach to Benghazi — where a Turkish warship made a landmark port call in 2025, according to Defense News — signals that Turkey intends to hedge regardless of which faction prevails.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is racing to lock in its Libya position before US-backed unification reshapes the landscape. Fidan's visit to both Tripoli and Benghazi signals Ankara will not let its maritime and military foothold become collateral damage of a settlement it did not broker.

sections.heading: Turkey Requests US Permission to Transfer Cluster Munitions to Ukraine
sections.body:
Turkey has asked the United States for permission to re-transfer tens of thousands of cluster munition rockets, missiles, and artillery projectiles to Ukraine, Human Rights Watch reported on August 11. The proposed $256 million deal includes 12 M270 multi-barrel rocket launchers, 70 ATACMS ballistic missiles containing 66,500 submunitions, 2,524 M26 rockets with 1.6 million submunitions, and 47,000 M509A1 203mm artillery projectiles containing 8.46 million submunitions — over 10 million individual explosive submunitions in total, many dating from US-licensed production in Turkey starting in 1987.

The State Department notified Congress on August 6, 2026, stating that the US government 'is prepared to authorize this transfer' and noting that Turkey 'seeks to reduce its inventory of older defense articles to focus its financial resources on modernization and sustainment of existing systems,' HRW reported, citing the congressional letter. Ukraine already possesses similar munitions.

HRW criticized the transfer, noting the artillery projectiles were removed from US service in 1994 and calling them 'obsolete' and 'inaccurate and unreliable.' The munitions are banned under the Convention on Cluster Munitions, which 112 countries have joined — though neither the US, Turkey, nor Ukraine is a party. It remains unclear whether the Trump administration has made the national security determination required to bypass the US export moratorium on cluster munitions.
sections.whyItMatters: The deal lets Ankara offload aging stockpiles while deepening its defense relationship with Kyiv and Washington. If approved, it sends a clear signal that Turkey is consolidating its NATO-aligned posture on Ukraine — and that Washington is willing to bend cluster munition export rules for strategic partners.

sections.heading: Hormuz Deadlock Deepens as Brent Crude Tops $100
sections.body:
Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei said on August 11 that the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed 'until the United States changes its policies and accepts Tehran's conditions,' according to Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency, reported by Gulf News. Rezaei told China's ambassador that Washington must end the conflict, release Iran's blocked funds, and help end fighting in Lebanon and Gaza. He added that any Oman-Iran agreement on a shipping corridor through Hormuz would remain separate from the broader closure issue.

On the military side, US Central Command said a US Navy MH-60 helicopter fired on and disabled a Panama-flagged cargo ship, the M/V Vela Nova, that attempted to break the American blockade of Iran's ports — the third such enforcement action since the blockade was reinstated on July 14, Reuters reported. CENTCOM said it has redirected 55 ships and boarded two others.

The economic impact is mounting. Brent crude topped $100 per barrel on August 12, according to the Economic Times, as doubts over a US-Iran peace deal and attacks on two ships fueled supply concerns. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright claimed the seven-day average for oil shipments through Hormuz had risen to nearly 9 million barrels per day, with an additional 5-7 million barrels per day leaving via upgraded pipelines — totaling about 15 million barrels per day. Iran disputes those figures and says the strait stays shut.

Pakistan's defense minister said on August 11 that the US and Iran were 'close to some sort of deal' on Hormuz, Reuters reported, but also noted that talks had hit a 'fresh impasse' with new Houthi attacks on shipping compounding the impasse. Gulf stock markets closed lower on August 11 as optimism over a deal faded.
sections.whyItMatters: For Turkey, a net energy importer, sustained $100+ oil is a direct inflationary shock that complicates the central bank's disinflation fight. The Hormuz closure also amplifies the strategic value of Turkey's alternative energy transit routes — and underscores why Ankara's Mecca Pact commitments to Saudi defense matter in practice.

sections.heading: Russia Secures Syria Base Deal, Assad Sentenced to Death
sections.body:
Russia's Foreign Ministry said on August 11 that a deal reached with Syria on the future of Moscow's military bases at Tartus and Hmeimim is 'an important step' that will boost ties with Damascus, Reuters reported, citing RIA. Bloomberg reported that the Kremlin sees the agreement as securing a hub for projecting power into Africa — a critical link in Russia's logistical chain from the Mediterranean to Libya, the Sahel, and the Central African Republic.

Separately, a Damascus court sentenced former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad and his brother Maher to death in absentia on charges of murder, torture, and incitement to murder, Middle East Eye and AP reported. Former security official Atef Najib was also sentenced. The ruling formalizes the new Syrian government's break with the Assad era but creates an immediate tension with Moscow, Assad's primary patron.

The base deal matters directly for Turkey: Russia's continued presence at Tartus and Hmeimim means Moscow retains military leverage on Turkey's southern border, even after Assad's fall. It also means Russia's ability to project into Libya — where Fidan arrived on August 12 — remains intact, adding another layer of complexity to Ankara's calculations.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia's retained footprint in Syria is a constraint Turkey cannot ignore. Even with Assad gone, Moscow keeps bases that anchor its Mediterranean and Africa operations — and a direct line of influence into whatever government emerges in Damascus.

sections.heading: Mecca Pact Faces Its First Battlefield Test
sections.body:
Houthi forces struck Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery with a drone on August 8-9, starting a fire that Saudi emergency teams extinguished. Aramco confirmed the fire and said there were no casualties; Houthis claimed responsibility, calling it retaliation for Saudi military actions in Yemen, multiple outlets including Middle East Eye, Al Jazeera, and Gulf News reported. The strike was the second Houthi attack on the same facility within a month, according to MSN and WION.

Aramco has shut the 400,000-barrel-per-day Jazan refinery following the attack, the Arabian Post reported, with restart not expected before August 30, according to Hydrocarbonprocessing.

The attack came one day after the August 7 signing of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan, which stipulates that an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all. A Jerusalem Post analysis, cited by WebIndia123, called the pact's first test a failure: the alliance produced no visible response to the strike on a member's critical infrastructure. The Quint published an analysis arguing the 'Islamic NATO' label is misleading — the three partners face different primary threats and the agreement is a 'capability bargain' rather than a unified command structure.

Yahoo News noted that the pact is better read as a verdict on the reliability of US security guarantees — a diversification, not a divorce from Washington. Saudi Arabia did not invoke Article 5-style obligations, and no joint military response followed the Jazan strike.
sections.whyItMatters: The Mecca Pact's mutual defense clause looked formidable on paper. Within 24 hours, a Houthi drone demonstrated that the alliance has no rapid-response mechanism — and no shared threat assessment to activate one. For Turkey, this gap between rhetoric and capability is the key strategic takeaway.

sections.heading: Oil Shock Hits Turkey's Economy as Bank Profits Dry Up
sections.body:
Turkish companies are facing a finance drought as bank profits dry up, MSN reported, citing an analysis by Bernard Kennedy in Ankara. The piece noted that criticizing banks is a common pastime in Turkey's business community, but the underlying problem is real: as banks' profitability contracts, corporate lending shrinks, squeezing the real economy at a moment when energy import costs are surging.

The energy cost picture is stark. Jet fuel prices have surged from $85-90 per barrel to $150-200 amid the US-Israeli war against Iran, Reuters reported. Brent crude topped $100 per barrel on August 12 as Hormuz deal hopes faded. Turkey, a net energy importer running persistent current account deficits, is directly exposed to every dollar of upside in oil prices.

Gulf stock markets fell on August 11 as prospects for a US-Iran deal dimmed, Reuters reported. Turkish markets face similar pressure: higher oil widens the trade deficit, feeds inflation, and complicates the central bank's 37% policy rate stance. The lira's trajectory and the CBRT's next moves will depend heavily on whether Hormux reopens or the current pricing becomes the new baseline.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey enters the $100+ oil environment with banks already tightening credit and inflation still elevated. The convergence of external energy shock and domestic credit contraction is the kind of pincer move that can quickly erode economic stability.

bottomLine: Turkey's diplomatic portfolio hit full stretch on August 12: Fidan flew to Libya to protect Ankara's stake before a US-backed unification reshapes the landscape, a cluster munition transfer to Ukraine awaits Washington's green light, and Iran doubled down on keeping Hormuz shut — pushing Brent past $100 and tightening the economic squeeze on an already fragile Turkish recovery. Meanwhile, Russia's Syria base deal ensures Moscow retains leverage on Turkey's southern flank, and the Mecca Pact's first real test showed that mutual defense on paper is not mutual defense in practice.
